turns.prompt: A company keeps a single table employees(emp_id, name, dept_name, dept_floor), with the department's floor repeated on every employee row. What goes wrong when the Sales department moves to another floor, when you want to record a new department that has no employees yet, and when the last employee of a department leaves? How would you fix the design?
turns.answer: Storing the floor on every employee row creates an update anomaly—moving Sales requires updating every Sales employee and a missed row leaves inconsistent floor values; it also causes insertion and deletion anomalies because a department’s floor can’t be recorded until an employee exists and disappears when the last employee leaves. The fix is to normalize by creating a separate Departments table (dept_id, dept_name, dept_floor) and have Employees reference it with a foreign‑key dept_id.

turns.prompt: A teammate needs to check whether a customer ID is in an unsorted Python list of one million IDs. They say: "`if cid in ids:` is O(1) because it is a single line, so it beats any loop I could write; and if it ever got slow, I would just run binary search on the list instead." What is wrong with each of these two claims?
turns.answer: `cid in ids` does a linear scan of the list, so its time is O(n) (the same asymptotic cost as an explicit loop, just with a smaller constant factor). Binary search only works on sorted data; running it on an unsorted list could discard the half that actually contains the ID and give a false‑negative, so you’d need to sort first (or use a set) for fast membership checks.

grade.rationale: The candidate correctly explains that the membership check is an O(n) linear scan rather than O(1), and correctly notes that binary search requires sorted data to avoid false negatives. They also mention appropriate fixes such as sorting first or using a set.
